summary: Hydrilla, also called water thyme, is an underwater plant with long stems, up to 25 feet, that branch at the surface into thick mats. It is one of the world's worst aquatic invasive plants: it can grow in deep, dark water where most native plants can't, its stems can grow up to an inch a day, and its surface mats block sunlight and push out native plants. Its small, pointed leaves grow in rings of 3 to 10 around the stem.
history: Hydrilla is native to Asia. One form was imported to the U.S. as an aquarium plant in the early 1950s and was soon found in canals in Miami and Tampa; the form found in New York is believed to have come from Korea and was introduced separately decades later in the Potomac River basin.
seasons: In New York, hydrilla plants have both male and female flowers, set some seed, and survive the winter as underground tubers.

handling.text: Hydrilla spreads mainly by stem fragments, so even tiny pieces can start a new population. It is most often carried to new waters on boats, trailers and live wells, and as a hitchhiker on water-garden plants.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
